newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Newcrest says has Normandy paper loss.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Newcrest says has Normandy paper loss.

text.p: Newcrest Mining Ltd said on Thursday it was carrying a paper loss of A$107 million from its A$450 million investment in Normandy Mining Ltd and pledged not to undertake more corporate adventures of that kind.

"We have an investment that, right at the present moment, in conditions of weakish gold prices and weakish gold index, is underweight from our cost (price) by A$107 million," chairman Sir Roderick Carnegie told shareholders at the annual meeting.
Asked by a shareholder if the company could guarantee it would not launch further "corporate adventures," Carnegie said: "We ain't going to do it again."
Carnegie said it was easy in hindsight to criticise the Normandy investment as unwise, but he said the shares would only be sold into an improving gold market.
He also noted reports of strong U.S. interest in Normandy.

"We feel that in a return to more buoyant gold prices, we think there is a reasonable chance that we exit the Normandy investment the way that ties in with Normandy's own desire to increase more of the shareholding of Normandy being owned by people in the United States," Carnegie said.
Normandy said on Wednesday it was considering to establish a presence in north America, through listing its shares on a stock exchange in the region and through possible operational links.
Carnegie said Newcrest did not stand to make a dramatic profit from the Normandy investment.

Newcrest first bought into the Normandy group in February and orginally opposed Normandy's A$4 billion group merger, but later agreed to Normandy merger associated companies after possible merger talks between Newcrest and Normandy broke down.
Normandy shares closed one cent lower on Thursday at A$1.77, which values Newcrest's 12 percent stake in Normandy at A$341.67 million. Newcrest shares ended five cents up at A$4.52.
Newcrest managing director John Quinn told reporters after the meeting that Carnegie's comments were not meant to rule out any further merger attempts.
"I think that the chairman was speaking about circumstances similar to those that we encountered to the Normandy situation. It is something we are not going to do again," Quinn said.
Quinn denied the company's relations with investors was still damaged by the Normandy affair and said the board went into Thursday's meeting with the backing of a large number of shareholders.
